text.tspan: Protocol fact
tools/list returns a flat array of {name, description, inputSchema}.
No namespaces. No subtools. Prefixes are convention only.
The granting test
"Would I ever grant one and deny the other?"
YES -> two tools. NO -> it is a parameter.

g.text: Accepted surface — one tool per separately-grantable operation

text.tspan: REJECTED — the mega-tool
platform_document(action: create|update|delete|search, params: object)
· one description must cover four behaviours: selection degrades
· inputSchema collapses to an untyped object: validation gone
· authorization becomes all-or-nothing — cannot grant read, deny delete
REJECTED — the passthrough
http_request(url, method, body)
The server holds three app tokens and will spend any of them
on any URL the caller names. That is a CONFUSED DEPUTY:
the authority is the server's, the intent is the caller's.
When the flat list gets long
The answer is NOT to collapse tools into an action argument.
It is progressive disclosure: tools/list_changed plus a search tool,
so schemas load on demand. (This session runs that pattern —
most tools are deferred names until searched for.)

g.text: READ set — safe to grant broadly
WRITE set — granted deliberately, per client

text.tspan: Deliberately ABSENT
outline_delete_document
vikunja_delete_project
A capability you never expose
cannot be misused, prompted into,
or mis-scoped later.
Credential aggregation
One process now holds Outline + Vikunja + Kavita tokens.
Compensating: tokens server-side only, never in model context;
narrowest scope each app supports; egress NetworkPolicy; per-call audit.
Indirect prompt injection
A document read out of Outline can contain instructions.
Tool OUTPUT is untrusted data, never instruction.
Write tools stay behind client-side confirmation.
Over-broad grant
Mitigated structurally: read/write split, absent destructive verbs,
authorization keyed on tool NAME rather than on a runtime argument.
collapsing these
loses the boundary
generalising these
loses the boundary
